newsitem.title: CANADA: Air Canada says Airbus fleet lowers costs.
newsitem.headline: Air Canada says Airbus fleet lowers costs.

text.p: The eight Airbus Industrie jets ordered by Air Canada will lower Air Canada's operating costs by at least C$20 million a year once the aircraft are all in service, the airline said on Friday.
Six of eight A330 jets ordered by Air Canada on Friday will replace the carrier's six Boeing 747-100/200 jets in 1999 and 2000.
"The C$20 million is a steady state after we get all six (747s) replaced, so that won't come until the year 2000," Chief Financial Officer Robert Peterson told a conference call with reporters.
Peterson said the three older 747-100s would likely be scrapped, but the 747-200s could be sold for US$20 million to US$25 million each in 2000.

Air Canada Chief Executive Lamar Durrett said Air Canada paid less than the $1.4 billion list price for the Airbus jet order announced today, but he declined to give details on the size of the discount.

Peterson said the order would add to Air Canada's "total leverage situation," but because the aircraft would have a positive impact on cash flow and would lower costs, the carrier would have greater ability to manage that leverage.
Peterson said Air Canada's long-term debt level was about C$2.4 billion on August 1, down from C$2.77 billion at June 30.
"In the month of July, we paid down about C$300 million of debt," he said.

Peterson said Air Canada was finalizing agreements on about C$500 million of bank credit lines, which when added to cash, would maintain the airline's cash and cash equivalent liquidity at the target level of about C$1 billion.
All excess cash beyond that C$1 billion level resulting from cash generated by operations or asset sales would be used to lower debt, he said.

Air Canada is not planning to issue equity to help fund the Airbus order, and as the purchase dates approach, the carrier will use a combination of cash flow and external financing such as aircraft lease facilities to pay for the planes.
Durrett said Air Canada enjoyed an "absolutely terrific competition" between Airbus and Boeing for the jet order.

"It was interesting after Boeing had won these 20-year exclusive contracts with American, Delta and Continental, Airbus, I think, really did feel the strain and the need not to lose another major North American client," he said.

Both manufacturers had "great products," but Air Canada obtained the Airbus jets at a good price under an agreement giving it flexibility to defer buying the 20 planes under option because of economic or other factors, he said.
Durrett said Air Canada planned to refurbish and keep 15 of its 32 DC-9s to use as operational spares or as additional capacity when needed, while the balance were on the market for sale.
Durrett said Air Canada planned to expand its cross-border flight schedule this year.
"We will have some additional announcements before the end of this month on new flights into the U.S.," he said.

Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Societe Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz AG unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
